identity.plain_name: Two pegs on one part that drop into a round hole and a slot on the other part, so the parts only go together one way, line up exactly, and still fit even if the holes are not spaced perfectly
identity.term: Locating pins with hole-and-slot location (round pin in a hole plus pin in a slot, or round pin plus diamond pin)
aliases: locating pins, locator pins, alignment pins, positioning pins
dowel pins used as locating features; dowels; parallel pins (ISO 2338; hardened: ISO 8734)
round pin and diamond pin; diamond locating pin; relieved locating pin; round-and-diamond pin location
hole and slot; pin and slot; dowel hole and dowel slot; slotted hole (for one of the two pins)
concentric locator plus radial locator (fixture-design terms for the round pin and the pin that stops rotation)
bullet-nose pins, cone locator pins, floating locating pins (variants with lead-in tips or sideways float)
tooling holes and tooling pins (circuit boards, sheet metal and assembly fixtures)
dowel connectors / plug connectors (PrusaSlicer 'Cut' tool, for split 3D prints)
spigot, register, pilot or pilot boss: a short round boss on one part that fits a matching bore in the other to centre it (Hobby-Machinist forum 'Register')
identity.one_liner: Two pins on one part fit into a snug round hole and a slot on the other: the round hole fixes the position, the slot (pointing along the line between the pins) only stops the part turning, so the parts line up in exactly one position and still go together when the hole spacing is slightly off.
identity.complexity: A few parts: two pins (usually hardened steel dowel or locating pins pressed into one part, or pins printed on it); a matching snug round hole and a slot in the other part (or two round holes with one round pin and one 'diamond' pin that has its sides ground away); plus separate bolts, clamps or a latch to hold the parts together.
identity.how_it_works: A pin in a close-fitting round hole stops the part sliding in any direction across the joint face, but it can still spin around that pin. A second pin stops the spinning, but if it also sat in a tight round hole, the distance between the two holes would have to match the distance between the two pins exactly; in real parts it never does, so the parts jam or bend (the joint is over-constrained). Making the second hole a slot that points at the first hole, or using a diamond pin that only touches its hole on two narrow curved lands, lets the second pin slide a little along the line between the pins while still blocking rotation. The flat faces pressed together fix the remaining directions (height and the two tilts), and bolts or clamps hold the parts together, so the part sits in one position every time without strain. A related centring feature is the spigot or register (pilot boss): a short round boss on one part fits a close bore in the other, so the parts share one axis and the screws only clamp them together. Screw threads don't centre a part on their own ('threads are considered non-self centering so you need something to make it run concentric, the register', Hobby-Machinist forum), which is why lathe chuck backplates and stepper-motor faces have one. A spigot sets the centre but not the angle, so a pin, slot or the bolt pattern stops the part turning.

job: line parts up exactly: puts a removable part, cover, fixture, jig or split 3D print back in the same place every time, and only one way round
join and hold: only partly; the pins carry sideways (shear) loads and take them off the bolts, but bolts, clamps, glue or magnets must hold the parts together
finder_attributes.motion: none once assembled; the part is lifted straight off the pins along their length
finder_attributes.degrees_of_freedom: 0 when seated and bolted down: the pin in the round hole removes the two sideways slides, the pin in the slot removes the turning, and the flat faces pressed together remove up-and-down and the two tilts; the one remaining freedom (lifting straight off) is closed by bolts, clamps or gravity. With two tight round holes, the turning is stopped twice over, which is why it jams (Carr Lane; MistyWest).
special_behaviour: self-aligning or self-centring: with chamfered holes and chamfered, tapered or bullet-nosed pin tips, a part set down slightly off slides onto the pins (Carr Lane bullet-nose and cone locator pins; Forerunner 3D chamfer tip)
none of the other listed behaviours; its own trick is tolerance absorption: the slot, a diamond pin or a floating pin lets the pin spacing be slightly wrong without jamming or bending the parts
finder_attributes.holding_principle: shape (form-fit: the pins sit in the hole and slot, which sets the position and resists sideways sliding and twisting), together with a separate hold-down by friction or clamping (bolts, clamps), spring force or gravity. The pins on their own do not stop the parts pulling apart.
finder_attributes.removability: removable: the located part lifts off once its bolts or clamps are undone (tool-free if it is only held by gravity or a latch); the pins themselves are usually pressed in (semi-permanent) or held by a lockscrew in a liner bushing so worn pins can be replaced (Carr Lane)
finder_attributes.reuse_cycles: many times: hardened steel pins in steel or bushed holes last a long production life, and replaceable pins in hardened liner bushings are used for long runs or heavy wear (Carr Lane); pins made of soft material wear out much faster than hardened ones (MISUMI), and printed plastic holes and pins wear and loosen sooner
finder_attributes.tools_needed: none to put the part on or take it off (apart from its bolts or clamps); to make: drill plus reamer for accurate pin holes, end mill or slot drill for the slot, hammer or arbor press to press pins in; for 3D prints, a drill or reamer to size printed holes and a vice or mallet to press in steel dowel pins
finder_attributes.load: Medium to heavy in sideways shear for steel pins (dowels help take heavy loads off the bolts holding the parts together, Forerunner 3D), but no strength along the pin: the parts simply pull apart unless bolted or clamped. Light for printed plastic pins, which snap easily, especially when printed standing up so the layer lines run across the pin. The pin in the slot only resists turning, so sideways loads are carried mainly by the round pin.
finder_attributes.adjustable: No: the whole point is one fixed, repeatable position. The slot absorbs small spacing errors automatically, and a floating locating pin can shift up to 1/8 in (about 3 mm) in one direction to cope with larger spacing variations (Carr Lane), but the located position itself is not meant to be adjusted.
finder_attributes.play_and_precision: Small play, set by the clearance between pin and hole: a 5 mm metric dowel (m6 tolerance) in a slip-fit hole made to +0.012/+0.024 mm gives about 0 to 0.020 mm clearance (Weinberg), and a dowelled engine-block joint repeated to about 5 micrometres (Slocum). Bolts alone in clearance holes let parts shift much more (an M6 bolt in a 6.6 mm hole has about 0.6 mm of slop). Printed holes and slots need more clearance (Hubs lists 0.5 mm tolerance for FDM interlocking parts, 0.2 mm for SLA and SLS), so expect a few tenths of a millimetre of play unless the holes are reamed to size [uncertain: no measured figure for printed hole-and-slot joints found]. Tolerates hole-spacing errors along the slot (up to the slot's length), but not errors across it, and only a little tilt, so holes must be square to the face.
finder_attributes.access_needed: one side only (blind): the part is set onto the pins from one side; a worn press-fit pin is easiest to knock out from the back through a through-hole (MISUMI recommends press-fit shanks where the back of the plate can be reached, and an air-vent flat for blind holes)
finder_attributes.materials: Pins: hardened tool steel (e.g. O1 hardened to 60-63 HRC) or case-hardened carbon steel (1045, 45-50 HRC); 300-series or hardened 400-series stainless where rust is not acceptable; hard coatings such as hard chrome or TiCN for corrosive places (MISUMI). Standard dowel pins: unhardened parallel pins to ISO 2338, hardened to ISO 8734. Parts located: metal plates and castings, wood, plastic mouldings, sheet metal, circuit boards and 3D prints; in 3D prints use steel dowel pins (or printed pins for light duty) in printed, drilled or reamed holes.
finder_attributes.maker_difficulty: easy for 3D prints, laser-cut sheet and wood: model or drill one snug round hole and one slot, and push in steel dowel pins; moderate for precise metalwork, which needs accurately placed reamed holes and a milled slot

processes: 3D print (FDM): model a snug round hole and a slot (or print the pins on one part); press in steel dowel pins for accuracy and strength
3D print (resin): tighter, more accurate holes; still better with steel pins
CNC: drilled and reamed pin holes, milled slots, fixture plates with locating pins
laser cut: round hole and slot cut into sheet parts and panels
sheet metal: punched round (or diamond-shaped) hole and slot in covers and panels
woodwork: dowels and pins in jigs and knock-down parts
off-the-shelf part: dowel pins, round and diamond locating pins, bullet-nose and cone pins, floating pins, liner bushings
making.print_in_place: no: the two parts are printed separately and put together; the pins are either printed onto one part or, better, separate steel dowel pins pressed into printed holes
making.making_tips_3d_printing: Use exactly two locating features: more than two pins generally over-constrains the parts so they go together badly or not at all (Forerunner 3D). If the two pins are closer than about 4 in (100 mm), two true round holes usually work; farther apart than that, turn one hole into a slot so the printer's size errors are absorbed, and point the slot at the other hole (Forerunner rules 1-3; Weinberg). Make the slot at least 0.125 in (about 3 mm) longer than the pin, or 0.05 in (about 1.3 mm) if space is tight (Forerunner rule 4). Printers usually print holes a little off size, so print a hole-size gauge first (e.g. the Printables 'Hole Tolerance Gauge', 3-8 mm holes with +0 to +0.3 mm steps) and design to what fits; for an exact press or slip fit, undersize the hole by about 0.025 in (0.6 mm) and ream it after printing (Forerunner rule 5). Allow clearance for the process: Hubs lists about 0.5 mm for FDM interlocking parts and 0.2 mm for SLA/SLS; Formlabs suggests 0.2 mm gaps for small parts and up to 0.4 mm for larger, chunkier ones on its SLA and SLS printers. Chamfer the pin tips and hole mouths: chamfers guide the parts together, let the pins print in more orientations and make them less brittle (Forerunner bonus tip; Slant 3D via Hackaday). Printed pins are weakest across the layers: CNC Kitchen's hooks printed standing up held only 55% (PLA) and 46% (PETG) of the load of hooks printed lying down, so print pins lying flat, print fins instead of thin pins, or better, use steel dowel pins. Put the two pins as far apart as the part allows so small position errors cause less angle error (Carr Lane). If a pin goes into a blind hole, give trapped air (and glue) a way out, such as a flat along the pin or a vent hole (MISUMI). In a printed jig, you can build rounded or diamond-shaped locators into the jig itself; Formlabs notes these reduce binding by touching over a smaller area. For split prints, PrusaSlicer's Cut tool can add dowel or plug connectors with a tolerance setting; remember that these use two round holes, so for long parts consider editing one into a slot in CAD.
making.off_the_shelf_parts: Dowel pins (parallel pins; hardened ISO 8734, unhardened ISO 2338); round locating pins (plain or shoulder type, press-fit or lockscrew type); diamond locating pins (relieved pins) in matching sizes; bullet-nose pins and bullet-nose dowels; cone locator pins with bushings; floating locating pins; locating pin liner bushings and lockscrews; stepped (double-pilot) pins; locating plugs for large holes; H7 reamers and slot drills or end mills for making the holes and slots. Suppliers such as Carr Lane and MISUMI (brands) sell configurable pins in custom head diameters.
rules_of_thumb: Use one round pin in a hole plus one pin that only stops rotation (a diamond pin, or a pin in a slot); two round pins in two round holes locate the rotation twice and bind during loading (Carr Lane, https://www.carrlane.com/engineering-resources/technical-information/manual-workholding/locating-devices/locating-pins and https://www.carrlane.com/product/locating-pins/locating-pins/round-diamond-locating-pins-lockscrew-type; Slocum 2010, author's manuscript p. 13, https://web.mit.edu/2.70/Reading%20Materials/Kinematic%20coupling%20review%20article.pdf).

Lay the slot along the line between the two pin positions and make it long enough to catch the pin wherever the hole spacings fall within both parts' tolerances (Weinberg, https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/simple-design-guide-alignment-dowels-steven-weinberg; Forerunner 3D rule 3, https://forerunner3d.com/design-guide-for-using-dowel-holes-in-3d-printed-parts/).

A diamond pin has four machined flats leaving two contact lands, each usually about one-third of the diameter wide; it must be turned so its lands stop rotation about the round pin, i.e. its long axis at right angles to the line between the pins, or the part can swing around the round pin (Carr Lane locating-pins guide, Figs. 7-7 and 7-8; Mechanical Design Handbook blog, https://mechanical-design-handbook.blogspot.com/2025/12/the-engineers-guide-to-precision.html).

Space locators as far apart as practical: Carr Lane shows that a 0.001 in position error barely matters when locators are far apart but significantly shifts the part when they are close together (Carr Lane, Figs. 3-12 and 3-13, https://www.carrlane.com/engineering-resources/fixture-design-principles/locating-clamping-principles).

Size a locating pin from the hole's maximum-material (smallest) size, a little under it: for a hole of 0.500-0.510 in, a pin of about 0.4995 in (Carr Lane, Figs. 3-20 and 3-21, https://www.carrlane.com/engineering-resources/fixture-design-principles/locating-clamping-principles).

Holder tolerances are typically 20-50% of the part's tolerances; making a tolerance twice as tight could make it about five times as expensive (Carr Lane, https://www.carrlane.com/engineering-resources/fixture-design-principles/locating-clamping-principles).

Standard metric dowels are made to m6: for a 5 mm dowel, a light press fit in the part that keeps the pin needs a hole of about -0.008/+0.004 mm, and a slip fit in the part that comes off needs about +0.012/+0.024 mm (converted from ISO H7/p6 and H7/h6) (Weinberg, https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/simple-design-guide-alignment-dowels-steven-weinberg).

3D-printed parts: two true dowel holes are fine closer than 4 in (about 100 mm); farther apart, make one a slot; slots at least 0.125 in (minimum 0.05 in) long; for exact press or slip fits undersize by 0.025 in and ream after printing (Forerunner 3D rules 1-5, https://forerunner3d.com/design-guide-for-using-dowel-holes-in-3d-printed-parts/).

Typical tolerances for interlocking 3D-printed parts: FDM 0.5 mm, SLA 0.2 mm, SLS 0.2 mm, material jetting 0.1 mm, versus 0.1 mm for injection moulding (Hubs, https://www.hubs.com/knowledge-base/how-design-interlocking-joints-fastening-3d-printed-parts/).

Do not rely on bolts to locate: an M6 bolt in a 6.6 mm clearance hole leaves about 0.6 mm of slop, which dowel pins remove (Mechanical Design Handbook blog, https://mechanical-design-handbook.blogspot.com/2025/12/the-engineers-guide-to-precision.html).

Pinned joints are good but not the best: replacing the dowels on an engine block's bearing caps with quasi-kinematic couplings improved repeatability from 5 to 1.5 micrometres, and split-groove kinematic couplings reduced pallet position variation by an order of magnitude compared with round-pin plus diamond-pin systems (Slocum 2010, pp. 13-14, https://web.mit.edu/2.70/Reading%20Materials/Kinematic%20coupling%20review%20article.pdf).

Spigot or register: make the bore as close a fit on the boss as you can without binding, and keep the mating face square to the bore so the part seats flat against it; the register 'provides most of the repeatability', so slightly loose threads don't matter (Hobby-Machinist forum 'Register', a moderator's answer, https://www.hobby-machinist.com/threads/register.82685/). Example: NEMA 17 motor brackets take a collar of up to 22 mm with screw holes 31 mm apart (VXB supplier page, https://vxb.com/products/42mm-nema-17-stepper-motor-mounting-bracket-with-m).

everyday_examples: car engine blocks, where the top and bottom halves of the crankshaft bearings (the bearing caps) are lined up with dowel pins (Slocum's example)
sheet-metal covers and service panels with one round or diamond-shaped hole and one slot over their locating screws, so they fit without forcing (MistyWest)
circuit boards with tooling holes (some slotted) that drop onto pins in assembly and test fixtures (I-Connect007)
large 3D prints cut into pieces and joined with dowels or plugs made by the slicer's cut tool

the round raised collar (pilot) on the face of a NEMA 17 stepper motor, which fits the centre hole of its mounting bracket; one supplier's bracket takes a collar up to 22 mm across, with screw holes 31 mm apart (VXB, a supplier)
a lathe chuck's backplate, centred on the spindle by a close-fitting register rather than by its thread (Hobby-Machinist forum 'Register')
guidance.when_to_use: Whenever two parts must line up the same way every time and come apart again: covers and lids, removable jigs and fixtures, tool plates and brackets, split 3D prints that are glued or bolted together, laser-cut or sheet-metal panels, moulds and casting patterns, and anything bolted together where the bolts' clearance holes would otherwise let it shift. The hole-and-slot version is the right choice when the pins are far apart, the parts are made with loose tolerances (3D printing, sheet metal, wood), or the parts are made of different materials that grow differently with heat. Use a spigot (register) instead when a round part such as a motor, flange, pulley or chuck must sit exactly on an axis; the screws then only clamp.
guidance.when_not_to_use: Not as the thing that holds parts together: add bolts, clamps, glue, magnets or a latch. Not when a part must return to within a few micrometres every time without any play: use a kinematic coupling (balls in V-grooves), which never jams. Not when parts must be guided in from far off-line: a self-centring cone and socket catches a bigger initial error. Not when the only goal is to stop a part going in the wrong way round: an extra offset pin or notch (keying) is simpler. For many small springy features sharing the job (e.g. mass-produced plastic parts), elastic averaging can be cheaper; for pins that must also lock, use a quick-release (ball-lock) pin or indexing plunger.
guidance.environment_limits: Steel pins in metal parts are stable over normal temperatures; where the two parts are different materials or change temperature, the slot (or a floating pin) lets them grow without binding, and cone locator pins are also used where parts expand with temperature (Carr Lane). Steel pins can rust; stainless steel or coatings such as hard chrome and TiCN help in corrosive places (MISUMI). Chips, dirt and coolant in the holes stop parts seating (Carr Lane). Printed plastic pins and holes soften with heat (PLA starts to give at about 60 °C, PETG at about 80 °C in CNC Kitchen's oven test) and creep under constant load, so press-fitted pins can loosen over time (Thrinter creep test).
guidance.safety_notes: Few hazards. Keep fingers out from between heavy parts as they are lowered onto the pins (pinch point), and wear eye protection when driving or pressing hardened pins. A standard dowel driven into a blind hole can be almost impossible to remove without drilling it out (Mechanical Design Handbook blog).
guidance.common_failures: (1) Binding or jamming because two round pins are used in two round holes, so the hole spacing must match perfectly; turn one hole into a slot or use a diamond pin (Carr Lane; Forerunner 3D). (2) Slot or diamond pin pointing the wrong way, so the part can still swing around the round pin; point the slot at the round hole and set the diamond's lands to stop rotation (Carr Lane; Forerunner 3D rule 3). (3) Slot too short to catch the pin when tolerances add up; size it for the worst case (Weinberg). (4) Too loose (the part rattles and lands in a different place each time) or too tight (it won't assemble); size pins from the hole's smallest size and choose standard fits (MistyWest; Carr Lane). (5) Printed pins snapping off along layer lines; chamfer them, print them lying down, or use steel dowel pins (Hackaday on Slant 3D; CNC Kitchen). (6) Pins in blind holes trapping air or glue, or stuck for good; add a vent flat or use through-holes (MISUMI; Mechanical Design Handbook blog). (7) Holes not square to the face, so the pins lean and bind; drill with a guide or drill press. (8) Wear and dirt: soft pins and holes wear and chips stop parts seating; use hardened pins, replaceable liners and keep the pins clean (Carr Lane; MISUMI). (9) Using the bolts to locate instead of pins, so parts shift within the clearance holes.
related: Split-part joints for large prints (alignment pins, dovetail keys, puzzle joints): the 3D-printing use of pegs and holes; this entry adds the hole-and-slot rule that stops long split parts jamming
Dowel and biscuit joints: woodworking dowels that align and strengthen glued joints; wood is forgiving, so two round holes usually work
Exact-constraint mounting (3-2-1 locating): the general rule behind hole-and-slot: use exactly as many contacts as there are ways to move
Kinematic coupling (balls in V-grooves): locates exactly with six point contacts and never jams; more repeatable than pins, but needs a hold-down force
Self-centring cone and socket (taper locator): catches a bigger starting error and centres with no play, but gives no rotation stop on its own
Keying (one-way-only fit, poka-yoke): an extra offset pin or notch that only stops parts going on the wrong way round; less precise
Elastic averaging (many-feature alignment): many slightly springy features share the locating job instead of two rigid pins
Indexing plunger (pull-knob index pin) and quick-release (ball-lock) pin: pins that can be pulled out by hand to lock or release a position
Drive-in fixing pins: roll pins, coiled spring pins, dowel pins and taper pins driven through both parts to fix them permanently, rather than letting them lift off
Pinned glue joint (pinning): a hidden pin glued into both parts, mainly to strengthen models and figures rather than to locate parts precisely and repeatably
Shelf pins and shelf supports: loose pegs in rows of drilled holes that a shelf rests on and can be moved between; they carry the shelf rather than locate it exactly
